intelligence.essence: External Guarantee Drift Law: every external guarantee supporting consequential NayaNET operations must remain scope-bound, versioned, evidence-backed, and revocable. Material changes or credible anomalies trigger proportionate qualification review and immediate containment where safety is uncertain. Provider restoration never restores authority automatically; independent requalification is required. Historical receipts and unaffected conclusions remain preserved. The measure of success is not merely noticing when a provider changes — it is that a provider can silently change, the monitor can investigate without inventing certainty, and affected workers lose the ability to rely on an obsolete guarantee the moment its qualification is withdrawn, even holding old instructions, cached certificates, or pending retries. Where changes cannot be detected promptly, rely on stronger independently enforced protections or limit the affected automatic actions. That is the boundary between monitoring drift and containing its consequences. The honest limitation is permanent: no finite scheme guarantees immediate detection of every silent change — so containment, not just detection, is the safety property.
intelligence.falsifier: A provider guarantee treated as permanent after one qualification; a silent change met with detection only and no containment; withdrawal and use-time fence not committed atomically; an invented drift start time; every operation in the exposure window blanket-marked duplicated; a restored provider automatically restoring authority; a single passing test presented as requalification; one broken guarantee erasing unrelated intelligence; a detection-time guarantee claimed without a complete observation and scheduling argument.

human_view.meaning: Trust in a provider has an expiration date — and the provider doesn't have to tell us when it changes. So we watch continuously and, more importantly, we build the system so that the moment we stop trusting a guarantee, nothing can act on the old trust anymore. Four things can silently change: the boundaries the guarantee covers, how long the provider remembers, whether simultaneous requests are still protected together, and whether new downstream side-effects appeared behind the same API. We track each with its own evidence, version the exact guarantee we're relying on, and run a state machine: qualified → needs review → suspected → suspended → requalified in a (possibly narrower) scope. When we pull a guarantee, the withdrawal and the enforcement lock in together — a worker holding yesterday's instructions gets rejected at the gate, even if it never heard the news. If we can't say when the change started, we don't invent a date — we mark the affected operations as needing review, one by one. And when the provider fixes itself, trust doesn't come back automatically: independent re-proof, new version, stated exclusions. The honest limit stands: we can't promise to catch every silent change instantly — so the real safety is containment. The moment trust is withdrawn, nothing consequential moves on the old guarantee.

intelligence.learning_lesson: This is the temporal dimension the provider stack needed: AER-PROVIDER-1 qualifies the contract, AER-DRIFT-1 keeps it honest over time. The permanent contributions: the detection+containment duality (detection can never be complete, so containment is the safety property), the four drift types, the versioned qualification manifest, the five-signals-plus-freshness monitoring with no averaging, the atomic withdrawal discipline borrowed from the Revocation Linearization Law, the exposure-window honesty rules, selective containment via the dependency graph, and the restoration-never-restores-authority rule. Every future external dependency inherits this: scope-bound, versioned, evidence-backed, revocable — or it doesn't support consequential action.

naya_view.directive: Version every provider guarantee with its exact scope, contract revision, and qualification revision. Monitor the five signals plus freshness; never average them into one score. Run the drift state machine with responses proportional to evidence, risk, and scope. Commit qualification withdrawal atomically with the use-time fence. Determine exposure windows honestly — never invent start times. Contain selectively through the material-reliance dependency graph. Require independent requalification after any restoration. Enforce provider qualification freshness at the governed commit boundary. Apply the detection budget by risk class; for unacceptable single duplicates, require stronger enforcement or prohibit automated uncertain-outcome retries.
